(* Each of ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ, NN64 and RR64 is the type of its values: asif at the type is the value itself, a typecase arm at its name takes its values and no other number type's, and a value's ilk is the type's name. *)
component NumberTypesAreObjectsWalk
export Executable

(* The arms at the five names that a value takes, one typecase for each name. *)
arms(x: Any): String = do
    inZZ32: String = typecase x of
            ZZ32 => "ZZ32 "
            else => ""
        end
    inZZ64: String = typecase x of
            ZZ64 => "ZZ64 "
            else => ""
        end
    inZZ: String = typecase x of
            ZZ => "ZZ "
            else => ""
        end
    inNN64: String = typecase x of
            NN64 => "NN64 "
            else => ""
        end
    inRR64: String = typecase x of
            RR64 => "RR64 "
            else => ""
        end
    inZZ32 || inZZ64 || inZZ || inNN64 || inRR64
end

run(): () = do
    a: ZZ32 = 7
    b: ZZ64 = 8
    c: ZZ = 9
    d: NN64 = 10
    e: RR64 = 1.5
    n: NN32 = 11
    f: RR32 = 2.5
    q: QQ = 1/3

    assert((a asif ZZ32) SEQV a, "a ZZ32 asif ZZ32 is the value itself")
    assert((b asif ZZ64) SEQV b, "a ZZ64 asif ZZ64 is the value itself")
    assert((c asif ZZ) SEQV c, "a ZZ asif ZZ is the value itself")
    assert((d asif NN64) SEQV d, "an NN64 asif NN64 is the value itself")
    assert((e asif RR64) SEQV e, "an RR64 asif RR64 is the value itself")
    assert((3.0 asif RR64) + 17, 20.0, "(3.0 asif RR64) + 17")

    assert(arms(a), "ZZ32 ", "the arms that a ZZ32 takes")
    assert(arms(b), "ZZ64 ", "the arms that a ZZ64 takes")
    assert(arms(c), "ZZ ", "the arms that a ZZ takes")
    assert(arms(d), "NN64 ", "the arms that an NN64 takes")
    assert(arms(e), "RR64 ", "the arms that an RR64 takes")
    assert(arms(n), "", "the arms that an NN32 takes")
    assert(arms(f), "", "the arms that an RR32 takes")
    assert(arms(q), "", "the arms that a QQ takes")

    assert(a.ilkName, "ZZ32", "the ilk of a ZZ32")
    assert(b.ilkName, "ZZ64", "the ilk of a ZZ64")
    assert(c.ilkName, "ZZ", "the ilk of a ZZ")
    assert(d.ilkName, "NN64", "the ilk of an NN64")
    assert(e.ilkName, "RR64", "the ilk of an RR64")
end

end

export Executable

(* A plain declaration at ZZ64 inside a generic one that returns its type parameter, its result below that of every instance it overlaps, is a valid overloading that loads, and each call runs the declaration that fits it. *)

pickFirst[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): T = a

run(): () = do
    w: ZZ64 = widen(4)

    assert(pickFirst(w, v), widen(5), "two ZZ64 values take the plain declaration, whose domain lies inside the generic declaration's and whose result ZZ64 is below T for every instance at T that holds a ZZ64")
    assert(pickFirst(z, y), 3, "two ZZ32 values take the generic declaration at ZZ32, which returns its first argument")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The checker and the one library

FACTS.md:169
- F-344 **Under walk, a value of the five native number objects or of the four string objects is read at its trait where walk infers a static argument, and walk's type text prints each of the nine by its trait.** `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` and `UnsignedLong` of `FortressBuiltin` read and print as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `NN64`; `FlatString`, `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` as `String`; also inside tuple types; each told by its declaring component (`interpreter/evaluator/types/LanguageTypes.java`), at `EvaluatorBase`'s three reads and in `FTraitOrObject.toString`. So `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, `Cell("s")` a `Cell[\String\]`, `<|1, 2, 3|>` an `ArrayList[\ZZ32\]`, and messages and `Reflect` print `ZZ32` where they printed `Int`; a float numeral, an `RR64` value (F-341), reads at `RR64`. The types keep their names: a `typecase` arm `Int` still matches `3`, and the ilk still names a string object by its own name, `FlatString`. Test: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-language-types/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

FACTS.md:159
- F-328 **Walk answers the compiled helpers `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv` with its own operations, and its ilk names the five native number objects by their traits.** The one library binds `Object.ilkName` to `stringOps.typeName` and `SEQV` over `Any` to `equality.sEquiv` (P-58's form); walk's loader maps the two names, before it looks for a helper, to `ObjectPrims$ClassName` and `AnyPrim$SEquiv` (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java`, `OWN_OPERATIONS`, a table that holds `runtime`'s six names too, F-335), so it never loads the two helpers. `Object.asString` is `self.ilkName`. Walk's ilk prints `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` and `UnsignedLong` of `FortressBuiltin` as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `NN64`, also inside static arguments, tuples and arrows; other types, strings, `Char` and `Ratio` among them, keep their names, and walk instantiates a generic at the trait (F-344). Tests: `tests/AnyNativesIntrinsicWalk`, `compiler_tests/AnyNativesIntrinsicCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-any-carrier/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

(** Returns a supertype of given type object that has a proper test generator,
    other than "constructed" one like `genAnyOf`.

    This routine is required for this kind of generic proprety:
    {{{
        propSomething[\T\](l:List[\T\], x:T): Boolean
    }}}
    If `T` were `FlatString`, a subtype of `String`, then `Arbitrary` factory would
    return `genString` which covers all values of `FlatString`, but `List[\FlatString\]` is
    not type-compatible to `List[\String\]` and we will get the unification error.
    Instead we have to convert every instances of `FlatString` to `String` at the first
    time --- this routine does so. **)
private adaptType(arb:ReflectiveArbitrary, t:Type): Type =
    if gen <- arb.genFromType(false, t) then
        if t2 <- findGenType(typeOf(gen)) then
            t2
        else
            fail("genFromType returned a non-generator " gen)
        end
    else
        t
    end

(** A generator for static arguments suitable for given generic type. **)
private object genStaticArgs(ty:GenericType) extends Gen[\Any\]
    getter asString(): String = "genStaticArgs"

    generate(c:TestContext): Any = do
        arb = c.arbitrary asif ReflectiveArbitrary
        tupleFromIndexed[\Any\](
            <|[\Any\] adaptType(arb, genTypeFromExtends(ext).generate(c))
             | (_,ext) <- ty.staticParams |>)
    end
end

531:\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
531: \section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
532: \seclabel{overloading-static-params}
533: 
534: The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
535: declarations without static parameters.
536: A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
537: type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
538: bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
539: A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
540: applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
541: round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
542: this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
543: A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
544: is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
545: following three rules:
546: \begin{itemize}
547: \item
548: The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to every
549: call to which the other is applicable.
550: \item
551: The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
552: specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
553: both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
554: \item
555: The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
556: every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
557: and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
558: is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
559: instance of $d_2$.
560: \end{itemize}
561: \revision{revival-overloading}{The revival's text of 30~September 2026 stated
562: the No Duplicates Rule as ``$d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than the
563: other'', which the strict sense of more specific above made refuse no pair.
564: It is stated on the relation without ``and not the other way round'', as the
565: type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 state it, and so it refuses
566: \EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)}
567: beside \EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket(x\COLON
568: \TYP{Box}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket)}, each applicable to every call to which the
569: other is.}
570: The Subtype Rule, the Incompatibility Rule and the Meet Rule above are these
571: rules for declarations without static parameters, with the conditions that
572: coercion adds; the Return Type Rule is the Subtype Rule's condition on return
573: types, checked over every instance of the less specific declaration and not
574: over one instance chosen for the pair.
575: 
576: As in \secref{more-specific-rule}, declarations of the set that are each more
577: specific than both $d_1$ and $d_2$ and that together cover every argument to
578: which both are applicable also satisfy the Meet Rule.
579: \revision{revival-meet}{The type group's paper of 2011 states the Meet Rule
580: without this case.}
581: 
582: Two parameter types with static parameters exclude each other, for the Meet
583: Rule and the Incompatibility Rule, as the type group's paper of 2011 decides it
584: by \emph{existential reduction}: each static parameter stands for any type
585: within its bound, and where the two parameter types, or their elements at one
586: position, are or extend instances of one parameterized trait, instantiation
587: exclusion (\secref{trait-types}) lets them meet only where the static arguments
588: of those instances are the same, every static argument but an operator argument
589: counting.
590: So where \TYP{Box} and \TYP{Pair} are distinct object types with static
591: parameters, the parameter types \EXP{\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
592: \EXP{\TYP{Pair}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket} of two declarations exclude each
593: other whatever \VAR{T}, \VAR{A} and \VAR{B} stand for.
594: \revision{revival-overloading}{The revival's text of 30~September 2026 read
595: instantiation exclusion here only where the two parameter types mention one
596: parameterized trait.
597: The type group's paper of 2011 reads it at every pair of instances of one
598: parameterized trait among the two types' supertypes, so that
599: \EXP{\VAR{copyOf}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(a\COLON
600: \TYP{Frozen}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)} and
601: \EXP{\VAR{copyOf}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(a\COLON
602: \TYP{Thawed}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)} exclude each other where
603: \EXP{\TYP{Frozen}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} and
604: \EXP{\TYP{Thawed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} both extend
605: \EXP{\TYP{Readable}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} and exclude each other, a value of
606: both having one instance of \TYP{Readable}.}
607:
